To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the water absorbed in collagen behaves as a single, broad, relaxation time distribution, which is temperature dependent, and that the distribution can be shifted to a single relaxation time at 23°C by a suitable choice of the frequency.
the dielectric constant of collagen decreases monotonically as a function of frequency, and the loss factor has a broad spectrum with no maximum.
the dielectric constant ε and the loss factor tan δ of water in collagen, at 23°C and for a frequency of 104 Hz, are 78 and 0.2, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dielectric properties of water absorbed in a biological macromolecule, namely, collagen.
the structure of water in collagen.
the structure of water absorbed by collagen.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relaxation process of water in collagen is characterized by an extremely broad spectrum, with relaxation times ranging from 10−5 to 10−10 sec.
water in collagen behaves as bulk water.

the dielectric properties of water in collagen can be interpreted in terms of the relaxation behavior of a single type of water molecule, which is characterized by an extremely broad spectrum (from 102 to 104 Hz) of relaxation times, with a mean value of about 104 Hz.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the relaxation times are distributed over at least 10 orders of magnitude and that the relaxation times increase with decreasing temperature, but the increase is not proportional to the decrease in the temperature.

water in collagen is characterized by the following features: (a) a large number of water molecules are bound to the collagen, (b) a large number are free to rotate, (c) there are two types of bound water, one with a high and another with a low dielectric constant, and (d) the bound water is characterized by a distribution of relaxation times.
water molecules are strongly immobilized in collagen, the relaxation times being of the order of 1 sec.
The main takeaway from our work is that
water in collagen behaves like a single component, and the water relaxation times are not affected by the presence of NaCl and HCl.
water absorbed in collagen behaves like water in a gel.
the structure of water in collagen differs markedly from that in bulk water.
